1:
Robertson explains why a council that had already condemned him met again: the night's action was illegal, so they felt the need of this ratification after dawn, which Luke 22:66 describes and which is the only session that evangelist reports. Lightfoot supplies the hour from the rabbis: the great Sanhedrin sat from the morning daily sacrifice to the afternoon one, and on a feast day such as this in the Court of the Gentiles; the seventy-one need not all attend, but three-and-twenty must be on the bench continually, so a man leaving had first to count his colleagues. Henry hears in the haste a reproach to us: they lost no time lest there should be an uproar among the people, and the unwearied industry of wicked men in doing evil should shame our backwardness in doing good — they that war against Christ and thy soul are up early, how long then wilt thou sleep, O sluggard?

On the binding both the ancient and the modern reader make the same correction. Bede grants the custom of delivering the condemned bound to the judge, but observes that they did not first bind him then, having bound him on taking him in the garden by night, as John declares; Robertson traces the sequence, bound at the arrest, sent on bound to Caiaphas, and bound again now, which implies he was loosed while before Annas and the council. Henry reads the cords as vestments: he was the great sacrifice, and sacrifices must be bound with cords, so Christ was bound to make bonds easy to us. In the handing over he sees the ruin of a church: by delivering up the king they in effect delivered up the kingdom of God, which was thus taken from them and given to another nation, since they betrayed him that was Israel's crown to them that were Israel's yoke. Theophylact says it shorter — they gave Jesus up to the Romans, and were themselves given up by God into Roman hands, that the word might be fulfilled which recompenses men after the work of their hands.

Of the single question Pilate asks, Robertson observes that it is the one charge out of all the Sanhedrin brought which he takes up: he does not believe it, but cannot pass over a man accused of rivalry to Caesar without becoming liable himself. Gill notes that the first question was put while the two were alone in the judgment hall, whither the Jews would not enter for fear of defilement. Bede finds their impiety exposed by the narrowness of the charge, since they could not even find a false accusation to bring, and reads the answer as framed to speak truth and yet give no handle for cavil. Theophylact leaves it more open still, the words being able to mean that thou sayest it, but I do not.

Gill lists what they heaped on him — that he was a magician and a blasphemer, that he made himself a king, forbade tribute to Caesar and moved sedition through the land — and Augustine gathers the same charges from Luke. Ellicott notes that many manuscripts omit the clause about his answering nothing, though the fact is implied in Pilate's question and in the statement that follows. Henry thinks the chief priests forgot the dignity of their place when they turned informers: wicked priests are generally the worst of men, since the better a thing is the worse it is when corrupted. Bede gives the reason for the silence: he would not clear himself, lest the judge acquit him and the gain of the Cross be done away. Theophylact says Pilate wondered that a man able by a word to destroy the accusations should instead bear them courageously; Robertson adds that Pilate had hoped for an answer to relieve him of the burden, and marvelled at the self-command he met instead.
6:
The custom is fixed by grammar and by season. Ellicott and Robertson both note that the verbs stand in the tense of habit, the governor's releasing and the people's asking alike. The Gloss gives the motive: Pilate did it to win favour, above all at the feast, when the whole province flocked to Jerusalem. On how many feasts, Gill records that the Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic read at every feast, though it belonged to the passover alone; Lightfoot adds that Beza's rendering at each of the feasts pleases him not at all, since Pilate says in so many words that he released one at the passover, a feast which carries in itself the memory of a people's release out of Egypt.

Of the man they preferred, the witnesses gather what makes the preference worse. The Gloss lists the aggravations — murder, committed in raising a sedition and disturbing the city, and notorious besides, since he lay bound with fellow rioters. Ellicott observes that Luke also calls him a rebel as well as a robber, but that Mark alone records the imprisonment of his companions. Robertson calls him a desperate criminal and leader of the rising, and draws the irony out: revolution against Rome was the very thing the crowd at Bethsaida Julias had once wanted Jesus to lead, so that priests and people chose a murderer in preference to him. Wesley adds that insurrection was the crime Roman governors, and Pilate in particular, were most careful to punish. Lightfoot sets beside him a famous rogue of the Talmudists, Eleazar Ben Dinai, whom they took to calling the son of a murderer, and Ben Nezer, the king of the robbers.

Bede reads Pilate's manoeuvres as so many openings for a release, the first being the setting of a robber against the Just One. Augustine harmonises the form of the offer: Matthew has Pilate name Barabbas or Jesus which is called Christ, Mark only the King of the Jews, but since kings were called Christs the two come to one, and Mark passes over Barabbas because he wishes to mention only what belonged to the Lord. Ellicott hears in Mark's phrasing a determination to fasten on the Jews the reproach that it was their own king he condemned, as afterwards in the title on the cross and the refusal to alter it. Robertson says Pilate rubs it in, the word then meaning since you have chosen Barabbas. Wesley asks which the wretched man betrays most, want of justice, of courage, or of common sense, since the coward sacrifices justice to clamour and enrages the very men he seeks to appease by repeating a title he knew they found offensive. Gill thinks him astonished that they should ask for so infamous a prisoner.

On the shouting Robertson notes that the priests shook the crowd up as an earthquake shakes, where Matthew has only that they persuaded them, and answers the puzzle of their fickleness: this was not yet the crowd of the triumphal entry, the plan being to finish the business before the Galilean sympathisers woke. Clarke says the word itself marks the bellowing of a multitude, a long loud cry such as Christ himself uttered on the cross. Theophylact sets their wickedness against the moderation of Pilate, and condemns him too for not resisting them, since he wished to satisfy the people, that is to do their will and not what was agreeable to God. Bede finds their refusal to answer the judge a fulfilment of the prophet's word that his heritage was become to him as a lion in the forest, crying out against him; and choosing a robber instead of Christ, they lost the country and the kingdom they had preferred to him. Pseudo-Jerome sees the two goats of the atonement, one loosed and sent away bearing the people's sin, the other slain for the sins of the forgiven.
15:
Robertson identifies the phrase for satisfying the crowd as a Latin idiom, to do what is enough to remove a man's ground of complaint, and reads Pilate plainly: he feared a crowd now wholly under the Sanhedrin's control, and knew what they would tell Caesar about him. Gill adds that he gave way only after washing his hands to testify his innocence. Henry sets the exchange as an accounting: Barabbas, the scandal of the nation, released, and Jesus, its glory, delivered up; and since Pilate had already persuaded himself to chastise a man he knew innocent, no wonder he could by degrees persuade himself to crucify him. Cyril of Jerusalem hears the prophet speaking beforehand in the person of Christ — I gave my back to the scourges — and finds the word answered when Pilate, having scourged him, delivered him to be crucified.

The hall and the robe are matters for the lexicon. Barnes glosses the Praetorium as where the governor sat to administer justice; Ellicott notes that it is another Latin word, Matthew's common hall; Robertson makes it the palace where the governor resided, and notes that Mark alone mentions the court inside it. On the colour the harmonists work harder. Gill says the robe was near enough purple to be so called, and was very likely one of the soldiers' old coats; Ellicott and Wesley judge that Matthew's word and Mark's indicate one colour, Tyrian purple not being far from scarlet. Augustine offers two ways out: the scarlet was used in mockery for royal purple, there being a red purple very like it, or the garment was scarlet with some purple about it.

Bede reads the dressing as a parody of royalty: because he had been called King of the Jews they put on him the purple which ancient kings wore, give a crown of thorns for the diadem and a reed for the sceptre, and bow the knee. Clarke doubts the thorns. Following Bishop Pearce, he argues that the Greek word may as well come from the plant the French call branche ursine, not of the thorny kind at all but soft and smooth, called by Virgil and Pliny a pliant herb grown in gardens and said to be common about Jerusalem; the crown, on that reading, meant derision rather than torture. Gill assumes the opposite, that the blow of the reed drove the sharp thorns into his temples; Barnes describes a circlet set about the temples rather than a covering for the head. Ellicott and Robertson note that the smiting, spitting and kneeling all stand in the tense of repeated action.

What the kneeling meant divides the readers. Bede takes the soldiers to have worshipped him as one who falsely called himself God; Barnes denies it, holding that the word carries no religious homage but only the honour done to princes, since they thought him madly claiming to be a king and not to be divine. Augustine settles the sequence instead, placing all this at Pilate's house before the leading out. Bede then turns the properties into allegory: the purple is the flesh he gave up to suffering and the thorny crown his taking on of our sins, while they smite the head of Christ who deny that he is very God, and smite it with a reed who would confirm that error out of Holy Writ. Pseudo-Jerome answers the mockery with exchange: his shame took away our shame, his bonds made us free, and by his crown of thorns we obtained the crown of the kingdom. Cyril of Jerusalem asks how they could spit on the face of him who by spittle had healed the blind. Theophylact turns it on the reader: we are called Christians, that is anointed, as kings were anointed, so let us put on that purple and walk as kings, and take that crown by a strict life and purity.
20:
The Gloss marks the turn of the narrative, that after the condemnation and the insults the Evangelist goes on to the crucifixion itself; Gill notes only that the soldiers had had enough of that diversion, and Robertson that Mark drops into the vivid present to lead him out. Augustine takes the harder question the procession raises. If Pilate gave him up about the sixth hour, as John relates, how could he be crucified at the third, as Mark says? He answers by measuring the hour rather than the instant: it was not yet fully the sixth when sentence was given, the fifth being over and part of the sixth begun, so that all which belongs to the crucifying falls between the end of the fifth and the completing of the sixth, by which time the darkness came.

Pseudo-Jerome sees every carried tree in Scripture walking out of the gate at once — Abel led into the field by his brother, Isaac coming forth with the wood, Joseph with his sheaf and the long robe steeped in blood, Moses with the rod and the serpent hung on the wood, the cluster of grapes borne on a staff, and Elisha's chip thrown in to seek the sunken axe, which is mankind, fallen to hell by the forbidden tree and swimming up to paradise by the wood of the cross. Bede works the same way on the man himself. Simon is called no citizen of Jerusalem but a Cyrenian, Cyrene being a city of Libya, so he stands for the Gentile nations, once strangers to the covenants and now joint heirs with Christ; his name is interpreted obedient and his city an heir, and he comes from a country place, which the Greek calls pagos, whence we name those aliens from the city of God pagans. So Simon carries the cross after Jesus when the nations leave their pagan rites and follow the steps of the Passion obediently.

On who bore the cross the two ends of the corpus meet. Theophylact observes that John has Jesus bearing it himself, and that both are true, since he carried it until someone passed whom they could compel; Robertson says the same from the other side, that Jesus bore his own cross till he was relieved of it and walked in front of it the rest of the way, and adds that Mark's word for compelling is the Persian term for impressed service. Lightfoot guesses why the soldiers picked him. The rabbis allowed wood to be fetched from the field on a feast day if bound up beforehand; he conceives that Simon came out so loaded, and that the sight of a strong bearer was itself the occasion, one burden exchanged for another.

The two sons are the puzzle Mark alone sets. Wesley says that Alexander and Rufus were afterwards eminent Christians, well known when Mark wrote; Clarke thinks the one likely the Alexander of the Ephesian riot and the other the Rufus Paul greets at Rome. Ellicott builds further on that. The detail, found in no other Gospel, is among the most striking marks of Mark's independence, and plainly had some special interest for him and his readers; the names are too common for certainty, but the Rufus chosen in the Lord who stands out among the Roman Christians, taken with the evidence tying this Gospel to that church, points that way — and if it holds, then since Paul calls the mother of Rufus his own mother too, Simon's wife must have come within the inner circle of Paul's friends, which suits the prominence Luke gives to men of Cyrene at Antioch. Robertson will have none of it: Paul does mention a Rufus, but it was a common name and proves nothing. Pseudo-Jerome draws the moral instead: as some men are known by their fathers' merits, this Simon is known by his sons'.
22:
Gill calls Golgotha an infamous place, noted for its many executions, and Henry compares it to Tyburn, so that in this too he was numbered with the transgressors; the name he takes from the skulls of malefactors cut off there. Two traditions attach to the spot, and Henry weighs them differently. That Adam was buried there he cannot credit, though he lists the great names who report it — Tertullian, Origen, Chrysostom, Epiphanius — and Cyprian's addition that many good people believe the blood of Christ trickled down upon Adam's skull, which they think congruous, since as in Adam all die, so in Christ shall all be made alive. The other he finds more credible, that Calvary was the mountain in Moriah where Isaac was to have been offered and the ram offered instead, so that Abraham had an eye to this day when he named the place for the Lord who would provide.

The draught offered him is described three ways and refused once. Gill says wine mingled with frankincense was what the Jews commonly gave to a man going out to die. Barnes observes that Matthew calls it vinegar, which fits if it was soured wine, the common drink of the Roman soldiers; Ellicott takes Mark's myrrh as partly explaining Matthew's gall; Robertson calls it myrrhed wine, and marks the difference, that Matthew says Jesus was unwilling to take it where Mark says he refused it. Of the parting of the garments Robertson notes a double interrogative found in Mark alone, who what each should take, and Wesley reads the order of the sentence as intimating that they nailed him first, parted the clothes next, and reared the cross afterwards.

The third hour against John's sixth is the knot of the chapter, and every hand tries it. Robertson cuts it by two clocks: Mark's third hour is Jewish reckoning and means nine in the morning, John's sixth is Roman and means six, which is when the trial was; Henry counts the same way. Barnes sets out the fourfold division of the day into watches of three hours, makes Mark's third nine o'clock and John's sixth noon, then points out that Mark professes to give the time exactly while John says only about the sixth hour; and he adds that a numeral was written not at length but as a letter, so that a copyist's slip is easy, the Cambridge manuscript having the letter here. Clarke presses that suggestion the other way, that John's sixth should be read third, the character for three being mistakable for the character for six, and cites Bengel, Newcome and Macknight for it; his own solution is that each of the four parts of the day takes the name of its first hour, so that the whole business of the crucifixion fell inside the division Mark calls the third. Calvin takes that principle and turns it to the other end of the interval: Mark means not the beginning but the close of the third hour, and it is highly probable that Christ did not hang upon the cross longer than three hours. Ellicott adds only that the precise hour is peculiar to Mark and agrees with the darkness at the sixth which all three report.

Lightfoot works instead on John's other phrase, the preparation of the passover, from which some have concluded that the eating of the lamb was put off that year to the fifteenth day, so that Christ ate his the day before while the Jews were still to eat theirs; On the board above the head the reports differ only in wording. Gill notes that the Syriac and Persic call it the cause of his death; Ellicott observes that Mark gives the shortest form of the inscription; Robertson collects the names, Mark's and Luke's word being the one behind our epigraph, where Matthew has accusation and John has title.
27:
Ellicott corrects the English at once: the men crucified beside him were robbers rather than thieves. Clarke supplies a curiosity from a copy of the Old Latin, which names them Zoathon on the right hand and Chammatha on the left. On the verse that follows, the textual critics agree and go further than Gill's bare citation. Clarke reports it wanting in many manuscripts, versions and fathers; Ellicott says nearly all the better manuscripts omit it, and that it probably began as a marginal note pointing to the prophecy our Lord had himself quoted as about to be fulfilled — adding that, were it genuine, it would be remarkable as one of the few places where Mark dwells on prophecy at all. Barnes takes the words as they stand and guards them: to be numbered with transgressors does not make him one, nor mean that God accounted him a sinner, but that in the popular estimate and by the judge's sentence he was reckoned among them, dying the just for the unjust and remaining in his death, as in his life, holy, harmless and undefiled.

Cyril of Jerusalem builds a whole meditation on the pair. Both had been transgressors before, but one was so no longer; the first stayed a transgressor to the end, stubborn against salvation, and though his hands were fastened he smote still with his tongue, joining the passers-by who wagged their heads. The other rebuked the reviler, and for him it was at once the end of life and the beginning of restoration. Cyril gives him a speech: I say not remember my works, for of these I am afraid; every man has a feeling for his fellow-traveller, and I am travelling with thee towards death, so remember me thy fellow-wayfarer — and not now, but when thou comest in thy kingdom.

That Mark and Matthew make both robbers revile is the difficulty, since Luke has one rebuke the other. Augustine solves it by grammar: the two, touching only slightly on this place, put the plural for the singular. Theophylact offers the alternative that saves the letter, that both reviled at first, and then one, recognising his innocence, rebuked his fellow. Robertson records the gap, that neither Mark nor Matthew gives the story of the robber who turned to Christ.

The mockery itself is met with its own answers. Ellicott notes that the interjection Mark records is a sort of inarticulate scorn found in no other Gospel, another instance of his habit of reproducing the very sounds uttered; that the clauses should be inverted, come down and save thyself; and that the taunt names not Christ but the Christ, the word not yet worn down into a name. Robertson observes that they turn his own language against him, using the very words he had used in calling men to see and believe, and that the tense shows they did it again and again. Gill reads the priests' mockery as laughing at one another, as the Syriac has it, their revenge satisfied. Bede turns the taunt round: in saying he saved others they confess against their will that he saved many, so their own words condemn them. Theophylact finds the devil behind the demand, who knew that salvation was being won by the Cross and pressed him to come down and undo it; but he did not, for had he needed to come down he would never have gone up at all. Pseudo-Jerome sees the foal tied to the vine and the garments dyed in the blood of the grape, while the kids tear at the vine and wag their heads; and he presses the unbelief home — afterwards they saw him risen from the grave, who would not believe he could come down from the tree, though it is far more wonderful that a dead man should rise than that a living one should step down.
33:
Gill and Robertson fix the sixth hour at noon, three hours after the nailing, and Clarke reckons the darkness to have lasted some two hours and a half, ending when he expired at the ninth hour, about the time the paschal lamb was sacrificed. Theophylact forestalls the natural explanation: had it fallen at the season for an eclipse someone might have called it a thing of course, but it was the fourteenth moon, when no eclipse can fall. Bede reads it as a withdrawal of courtesy — the most glorious light took back its rays lest it should see the Lord hanging, and lest blasphemers should have the benefit of its shining — and finds the hour significant, since Adam heard God walking in paradise in the cool after midday, so that in the very hour when the first Adam brought death into the world, the second destroyed it by dying. Henry takes the darkness for the sign from heaven the Jews had so often demanded, granted at last but signifying the blinding of their own eyes, since they were labouring to put out the Sun of righteousness; what could follow but a darkness worse than the Egyptian?

On the cry the philologists work first. Lightfoot observes that Matthew keeps the very syllables of the psalm while Mark gives the word in the current Chaldee; Ellicott says the same, Mark reproducing the Aramaic sound and Matthew the Hebrew as written. Robertson notes a variant which reads reproached for forsaken, and will not pretend to measure the desolation, only insisting that he did not thereby cease to be the Son of God, which were impossible. Wesley holds both halves together: he claims God as his God even while lamenting that his Father withdrew the tokens of his love and treated him as an enemy while he bore our sins. Bede answers those who stumble at the lowliness of the words. Hunger and thirst and weariness were not proper to the Divinity but bodily afflictions, and so was this voice, since a body never wishes to be parted from the life joined to it; he spoke as man, carrying our feelings about with him. Theophylact adds that he spoke for us, who have been forsaken as he never was, since he could say he was not alone because the Father was with him.

The mishearing is explained the same way by ancient and modern. Robertson says they took the word for God to be the name of Elijah; Bede supposes them Roman soldiers who did not know the peculiarity of the Hebrew tongue. Augustine harmonises the reports, that Matthew has the others speak of Elias while Mark gives it to the man with the sponge, from which we gather that both said it. Calvin works the same seam: John gives the words to the soldier with the vinegar and Matthew to others, which is no inconsistency, since the jeer was begun by one and eagerly caught up by the rest; and the phrase implied not restraint but ridicule, every man singing the same song to his neighbour, as men do who are agreed upon a course.

Pseudo-Jerome makes the properties speak. The sponge on a reed is weak, dry and fit for burning, and they fill it with vinegar, that is with guile; but we who are of the earth die with a low voice or none at all, while he who came down from heaven breathed his last with a loud one. Theophylact hears the same power in it: he who rules death and commands it dies as its Lord, and Luke tells us what the voice said, that he commended his spirit into his Father's hands — by which we understand that from that time the souls of the saints go up into the hands of God. Robertson notes only that Mark's word means, literally, that he breathed out.
38:
The Gloss marks the hinge, that the Evangelist having told the Passion now turns to what followed it. Gill adds from Matthew what Mark omits, the earthquake at the same moment, the rocks rent and the graves opened. Theophylact reads the torn veil two ways at once: that the grace of the Spirit is rent away from the temple, so that the Holy of holies stands open to every eye; and that it figures the living temple, the body of Christ, whose garment, that is his flesh, is torn in the Passion, the rending reaching from Adam down to the latest man. Pseudo-Jerome puts it in one line, that the veil is rent, that is, heaven is opened — and that the last are now made first, since the Gentile confesses while the blinded Jew denies. Cyril of Jerusalem sets the whole under the epistle's figure: Christ being come a high priest of the good things to come, entered once for all into the holy place, not by the blood of goats and calves but by his own, and obtained eternal redemption.

The centurion's word is examined for its Latin and for its cause. Ellicott notes that Mark, after his manner, uses the actual Roman title where Matthew uses the Greek equivalent, and Robertson that the word stands nowhere else in the New Testament but here and a few verses on; he refers the opening so to the darkness and the earthquake, and prefers to render the confession a Son of God. Bede finds the cause of the wonder plain: seeing the Lord die in that manner, sending forth his own Spirit, he judged rightly, since no one can send forth his own spirit but the Creator of souls. Augustine sharpens it to the instant — what he wondered at most was that immediately after that cry the Spirit was given up; for it left the flesh not unwillingly but as it willed, being joined to the Word of God in unity of person, so that no penalty of sin had power to cause that death. Theophylact hears the order of the world inverted here: the Jew kills and the Gentile confesses, the disciples fly and the women remain.

The list of the women is compared with Matthew's. Ellicott finds it the same but for two things, the epithet little applied to James and the name Salome where Matthew has the mother of Zebedee's children; Robertson takes the two for one person, Salome being named in Mark only. Clarke records that some manuscripts read Joset or Joseph for Joses. Bede sorts out the James: he is the son of Alphaeus, called the Lord's brother because his mother was sister to the Lord's mother, the Mary of Cleophas whom John names beside the cross; and he is the Less, to distinguish him from Zebedee's son.

Of their ministering Bede observes that it was a Jewish custom, not thought blameable by that ancient people, for women to furnish teachers with food and clothing out of their substance; they gave him their carnal things whose spiritual things they had reaped, and so showed a pattern for all masters. Wesley glosses the service as providing him with necessaries, and Gill says they followed him wherever he went in Galilee and thence to Jerusalem. Robertson marks the two imperfect tenses that stretch the following and the serving across the whole Galilean ministry, and closes with the picture: these faithful women were last at the Cross, standing afar off and watching the end of all their hopes. Pseudo-Jerome answers that with a promise — as through the Virgin the female sex is not shut out from salvation, so through Mary Magdalene and the others it is not thrust away from the knowledge of the mystery of the Cross and the Resurrection.
42:
The Gloss marks the turn to the burial, and the rest explain the word Mark stops to gloss. Ellicott notes that the explanation is characteristic of an evangelist writing for Gentile readers, and fixes the sense of the word past doubt; Robertson makes it our Friday, which began at sunset. Bede gives the philology, that the Greek parasceue is the Latin praeparatio, the name by which Jews living among Greeks called the sixth day, since on it they made ready what the coming rest required. Barnes puts the even after three in the afternoon and says the coming day was of peculiar solemnity, so more than ordinary provision was made beforehand. Lightfoot asks why the name should be given at all, and answers that they made ready not so much themselves as their food, by the law that whatsoever ye will bake, bake today. Gill notes that the Syriac and Persic read it the night of the sixth day, Friday night.

The haste is explained by law. Clarke recalls that Moses had ordered no criminal to hang on a tree past sunset, and supposes Joseph feared the corpse might be flung into the common grave with the two robbers, and so entreated Pilate earnestly for it; Wesley says only that the bodies might not hang on the sabbath. Bede finds a whole week's theology in the day. Man was made on the sixth and the Creator rested on the seventh, so fitly was the Saviour crucified on the sixth and, resting in the tomb through the sabbath, waited for a resurrection on the eighth; and so must we be crucified to the world now, rest when the debt to death is paid, and in the eighth period receive our bodies back glorified.

Of the man who came forward the witnesses are unanimously admiring. Henry observes that a malefactor's corpse lay at the disposal of the government, and that those who hurried him to the cross meant him to make his grave with the wicked, but God meant him to make it with the rich, and so he did. Bede argues that the burier had to be both worthy by righteous merit and able by worldly rank, and unpacks the title: the counsellor is in Latin a decurio, of the order of the curia, holding a provincial magistracy; Arimathaea he identifies with Ramathaim, the city of Elkanah and Samuel. Theophylact praises the boldness as of the right kind, since Joseph did not stop to reckon that he would fall from his rich estate and be cast out by the Jews for begging the body of one condemned as a blasphemer. Pseudo-Jerome finds the name itself apt, being interpreted taking down, and reads the sequel as gain: by the burial of Christ we rise again, and by his descent into hell we mount up into heaven — here is the honey found in the mouth of the dead lion.

Theophylact accounts for Pilate's surprise, that he expected a man to linger on the cross as the robbers did, and so called the centurion to ask whether death had come before the usual hour. Joseph, he says, buried the precious body preciously, knowing as a disciple what honour was due to it — and he turns the burial into a rule for the reader: take the body of Christ to yourself by unity and lay it in a sepulchre hewn from the rock, that is in a soul recollected and never forgetful of God; wrap it in linen, that is receive it into a pure body. Pseudo-Jerome reads the same scene as the history of a nation: Israel, believing at the last, lays aside despair, waits for the kingdom of God and goes in to be baptized, while the elect look on from afar.
43:
Joseph's title is turned over by everyone. Robertson makes him a senator of high standing and wealth, and notes that the phrase for looking toward the kingdom of God uses the verb Luke applies to Simeon and Anna. Barnes insists the word rendered honourable is no mere name of office but a judgment on the man, and that his waiting meant more than the expectation every Jew shared, since it implies he already believed this was the Messiah. Wesley says the same shortly, a man of character and reputation, a member of the sanhedrim, who expected the kingdom set up on earth. Gill takes him for a priest of the bench that sat in what the rabbis call the chamber of the counsellors. Lightfoot works that chamber over: the Vulgate makes him a noble officer and Beza an honourable senator, while the Talmud says the room was first the chamber of the counsellors and became the chamber of chief men once the high priesthood was bought and changed yearly.

The boldness draws the warmest comment. Ellicott would render it that he waxed bold and went in, hearing an implied contrast with his former timidity; Clarke marvels that the coward now acts a more open part than any disciple, since it took courage to declare for one condemned hours before as a blasphemer by the Jews and a seditious man by the Romans — and he finds the reason where the apostle puts it, that we have boldness to enter the holiest through his blood, so that the death of Jesus is the grand cause of courage in a believing soul. Calvin fixes on the waiting rather than the daring. That Joseph looked for the kingdom of God is his highest commendation, and the root of the righteousness he is praised for, since no man dedicates himself to God unless he expects God to be his deliverer; and though the promise was made to all the Jews, the Spirit testifies this of very few.

Pilate's caution is treated as evidence. Gill and Barnes both explain the surprise from the nature of the punishment, which killed slowly — commonly in two or three days, Barnes says, and sometimes six or seven — and Gill adds that the two robbers were still alive when Christ was dead. Ellicott notes that the wonder and the summoning of the centurion are Mark's alone, the article showing him the same officer already named. Robertson calls the construction a classical idiom, our own I wonder if, and observes that Mark omits the request that the legs be broken; Pilate wanted an official report before releasing the body.

Of the burial Ellicott would read a fine linen sheet, and notes that only Mark says it was bought as the sabbath came on; Gill supposes the purchase made in the city. Robertson explains that the winding verb occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and that the participle for the hewing comes from the word for a stonecutter; Wesley adds that Joseph rolled the stone by his servants, it being far too large for one man. Cyril of Jerusalem puts the questions a catechist would ask — is the tomb built with hands, raised like the tombs of kings? — and answers from the prophets, who bid us look into the solid rock that was hewn, and say that they cut off his life in a dungeon and cast a stone upon him, so that the chief corner stone lay a little while within a stone. Barnes and Clarke both dwell on the watchers: the strong and the mighty had fled, and it was a timid man and a few weak women who owned him in death, such love showing its truth in the dark shades of adversity. Robertson lets the tense hold the picture, the two Marys watching in silence as the shadows fell across all their hopes.
